why: attachRecoveryWrap encrypts a fresh random key instead of the live data key. The recovery door then opens a different room than the password, so a diary sealed before the recovery code existed cannot be read after recovery.

why: The normalized recovery secret is stored on the lock next to the wrap. Anyone who can read localStorage then has the second door in plaintext.

why: Adding a recovery wrap deletes wrap. The password then cannot open a kdf-3 lock, so installing recovery locks the user out of the door they already know.

why: Adding recovery strips wrap and leaves kdf 3. A client that has never heard of recovery — the phone that has not updated yet — then treats the correct password as wrong.
replace: return { ...lock, wrap: undefined, kdf: 3, recovery: recoveryWrap };

why: The recovery wrap is returned without proving it re-opens. An unopenable wrap would still be persisted, and the user would be told they are safe.

why: A wrong recovery code deletes the recovery wrap. One typo then destroys the second door, and a later attempt with the right code has nothing to open.

why: Generating a recovery code also rewrites wrap. The password door then no longer matches what is on disk, which is a silent re-key of the wrapping layer.
replace: return { ...lock, wrap: lock.wrap ? { ...lock.wrap, iv: recoveryWrap.iv } : lock.wrap, recovery: recoveryWrap };
testName: generating a recovery code does not re-key the vault or modify wrap

why: The recovery code is drawn from Math.random instead of crypto.getRandomValues, so it is not a cryptographic secret.

why: mergeDiskVault keeps the local lock wholesale whenever one already exists, so a stale copy without recovery overwrites a disk copy that has it and the second door is gone after boot.
